Period schedule:

Total: 6 periods · 4h 0min

periods.activity_title: Reading the Poem and Activating Prior Knowledge

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.16): who inspires you? — brief oral warm-up.
Let us read (p.16): paired picture discussion — what can we learn?

time_bands.activity: Invite students to respond to the warm-up prompt from 'Let us read' (p.16): who or what inspires them to do their best? Take three or four quick spoken responses from volunteers to prime the theme of perseverance.

Students work in pairs to identify the six pictures on p.16 (honeybee hive, spider web, geese, weaver-bird nest, ants, apple tree) and share what lesson each creature or image suggests. Pairs report to the class in a quick round.

Teacher reads the poem 'Try Again' aloud at a measured pace (textbook p.16–18), with students following. Pause briefly after each of the three narrative movements — Bruce's despair, the spider's nine attempts, Bruce's renewal — to let the imagery settle. No comprehension questions yet; the goal is an unhurried first encounter with the poem's full arc.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's narrative ballad style means meaning builds stanza by stanza; resist interrupting the read-aloud with questions so students experience the mounting suspense the poet creates. The pre-reading pictures (honeybee, spider web, ants) are deliberately chosen to foreshadow the poem's central metaphor of the spider — let students surface that connection naturally. Self-study pointer: the picture-discussion task also asks students to share observations with classmates; those who did not get a turn in pairs can revisit the pictures independently at p.16.
materials: Textbook p.16–18 (poem text and pre-reading pictures)

periods.activity_title: Poem Comprehension — Summary, Central Idea, and Poetic Devices

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.19): fill summary blanks with words from poem.
Let us discuss (p.19): complete sentences on narrative style and central idea.
Let us discuss (p.19): why does the poet repeat 'tried and tried', 'up, up'?

homework.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.19): pick three lines describing spider's efforts and three examples of alliteration.

time_bands.activity: Students work individually to complete the cloze-summary from 'Let us discuss' (p.19), filling eight blanks with words from the box (tried, mounted, despair, attempts, great, conquered, low, strive). Teacher circulates, then takes class answers orally and confirms each word choice.

Teacher-led discussion on the two completion sentences from 'Let us discuss' (p.19): why is the poem in narrative style, and what is its central idea? Elicit student responses and build a shared statement of the central idea on the board.

Students write individual responses to the repetition question from 'Let us discuss' (p.19) — why 'tried and tried', 'steadily, steadily', 'up, up' are used. Share two or three responses aloud; teacher draws out that repetition enacts the perseverance the poem celebrates.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the poem aloud, students are ready to engage with its structure; anchor the central-idea discussion to specific stanzas rather than abstract statements. The poem's chief device is repetition — 'tried and tried', 'up, up', 'steadily, steadily' — which enacts the very persistence it celebrates; watch for students who describe repetition as merely decorative rather than purposeful. The alliteration and spider-description tasks (p.19) are assigned for self-study so that discussion time stays focused on meaning rather than listing.

periods.activity_title: Extract Analysis, Metaphor Work, and Listening to the Ant Story

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.21): Extract 1 — four questions on despair and imagery.
Let us listen (p.24): predict then verify five MCQs on the ant story.

time_bands.activity: Students read Extract 1 from 'Let us think and reflect' (p.21) silently, then answer its four questions: identifying the phrase showing the King's physical despair, explaining why the poet writes 'low despair', choosing the meaning of 'pondered', and selecting what 'silken filmy clue' conveys. Take answers as a class discussion, pointing back to specific lines.
Students read the five prediction questions from 'Let us listen' (p.24) and record their guesses before listening. Teacher then reads the ant story aloud at a steady pace from the transcript.

Teacher reads the ant story a second time; students check and correct their predicted answers. A brief class discussion compares the ant's experience with the spider's journey in the poem — both creatures persist against odds — before confirming the correct options.

periods.teacher_notes: The extract on King Bruce's despair (p.21) introduces close-reading of emotional language — students often paraphrase loosely, so press them to quote the exact phrase ('flung himself down in low despair') when identifying physical expression. The ant listening story was chosen because its theme of perseverance and teamwork mirrors the poem's message; draw that connection explicitly when debriefing the second listening. The Extract 2 questions (p.21–22) are richer than time allows here — flag them as strong self-study material at p.21–22.

periods.activity_title: Personal Narration and Letter-Writing on Perseverance

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.25): narrate a personal experience of perseverance using seven prompts.
Let us write (p.26): write a letter to cousin advising how to overcome difficulty.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly maps the seven prompt headings from 'Let us speak' (p.25) on the board — Introduction, Challenge, Feeling disheartened, Source of motivation, Action, Result, Reflection — and models a single sentence for the first two prompts so students see the structure.

Students take one minute of silent planning, then deliver their narrations in pairs; each partner speaks while the other listens. Teacher circulates and offers brief feedback on clarity and use of the prompts, then invites two or three students to share with the whole class.

Teacher introduces the letter task from 'Let us write' (p.26), displaying the given opening and closing lines and discussing the format — address, date, salutation, body with transition words, close. Students note the transition sequence (To begin with, Next, After that, Then, Finally) in their books.

Students draft the body of the letter independently, using the transition words to sequence their advice. They aim to complete a first draft and read it over for sense before the unit ends; teacher collects drafts or students keep them for self-review.

periods.teacher_notes: King Bruce's renewal of resolve at the poem's close is the imaginative springboard for both tasks — the speaking narration externalises a personal Bruce-like moment, while the letter asks students to articulate that advice to someone else. Watch for letters that state the steps without the advised transition words; the constitution of the task at p.26 makes the sequence of transitions an explicit requirement. The metaphor-to-simile transformation task (p.20–21) could not be accommodated here — it is a worthwhile self-study exercise at those pages.
materials: Textbook p.26 (Let us write task and format)

periods.activity_title: Vocabulary from the Poem — Opposites, Meanings, and Distance Words

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.22): write opposites of five words taken from the poem.
Let us learn (p.23): match meanings and frame sentences for endeavour, toil, strive, braced.
Let us learn (p.23): classify distance words and phrases as far or near.

time_bands.activity: Students locate the five words (up, fast, glad, win, succeed) in the poem and write their opposites from 'Let us learn' (p.22). Teacher takes answers quickly and confirms, noting that these pairs reflect the poem's own tonal movement from defeat to victory.

Students match the four underlined words (endeavour, toil, strive, braced) to their meanings from the box on p.23, then frame an original sentence for each word. Pairs compare sentences and the teacher selects varied examples for class sharing.

Teacher draws attention to the poem's distance language ('a long way up', 'inch by inch', 'half-yard higher') and then students classify the eleven distance words and phrases from 'Let us learn' (p.23) into Far and Near columns. Class discussion confirms the groupings.

periods.teacher_notes: The distance-words task (p.23) arises directly from the poem's spatial imagery — the spider's upward journey is measured in increments ('inch by inch', 'half-yard higher') — so pressing students to see that connection deepens both vocabulary and poetic reading. The tongue-twister activity (p.24) is a lively wordplay task that could not fit here; flag it as an enjoyable self-study and creative exercise at p.24. A common error is writing antonyms for 'win' as 'loss' (a noun) rather than 'lose' (a verb) — clarify the grammatical category.
materials: Textbook p.22–24 (Let us learn tasks I–III)

periods.activity_title: Spider and Ant Observation — Nature Connections Beyond the Poem

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.26): observe spider and ant differences, share with class.
Let us explore (p.26–27): weave a spider-web model with sticks and wool, decorate with poem words.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the fact that spiders are arachnids, not insects, using the note from 'Let us explore' (p.26). Students draw a simple comparison table in their notebooks — number of legs, body parts, web-making, relationship to the poem — and share two or three differences with the class.

Students follow the four-step web-weaving instructions from 'Let us explore' (p.26–27), tying three sticks together and looping wool to form a web. Teacher circulates and assists with the tying and looping steps.

Students decorate their webs by writing on small paper tags or directly on the wool: words and phrases from the poem that describe the spider's journey ('silken filmy clue', 'steadily, steadily', 'strong endeavour'). A brief gallery walk lets students see each other's webs and the words chosen.

periods.teacher_notes: The spider-and-ant comparison grounds the poem's central creature in factual biology, bridging English with science as the textbook suggests at p.26. The web-weaving craft is a hands-on extension of the poem's imagery — all materials (sticks, wool) should be assembled at the start of this unit so no time is lost. The folk-songs project (p.26, task I) could not be accommodated in a single sitting; flag it as an enrichment project students may pursue with their families or in the school library.
materials: Textbook p.26–27 (Let us explore tasks II–III)
Three short sticks per student (approx. 8 inches each)
A roll of wool or thick yarn per group
Small paper tags or pieces of card for decoration

items.source_lo: Student analyses a narrative poem's language, imagery, and structure using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: King Bruce's despair, spider's nine attempts, repetition devices, rhyme scheme, 'low despair', 'silken filmy clue'.
items.item_stem: Read the opening stanza of 'Try Again' on page 16, beginning “King Bruce of Scotland flung himself down.” Which of the following best describes the mood established in this stanza?

options.label: A
options.text: Curious and alert, as the King watches a creature climb the ceiling.

options.label: B
options.text: Despairing and heavy-hearted, as the King loses hope after repeated failure.

options.label: C
options.text: Joyful and celebratory, as the King prepares for a great victory.

options.label: D
options.text: Proud and determined, as the King resolves to try once more.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student has confused the poem's closing celebratory tone with the opening stanza's mood of failure.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has read ahead to the spider episode and conflated it with the stanza being asked about.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has mapped the poem's ending resolution onto the opening, missing the narrative arc.

items.source_lo: Student analyses a narrative poem's language, imagery, and structure using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: King Bruce's despair, spider's nine attempts, repetition devices, rhyme scheme, 'low despair', 'silken filmy clue'.
items.item_stem: In 'Try Again,' Eliza Cook repeatedly uses phrases such as 'tried and tried', 'up, up', and 'steadily, steadily'. Explain how this repetition does more than decorate the poem — what does it achieve in terms of the poem's meaning and the reader's experience of the spider's climb?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The repeated phrases enact the very persistence they describe — each doubling mirrors the spider's repeated attempts, so the reader feels the effort accumulating rather than simply being told about it. This builds suspense and makes the spider's eventual success at the cobweb door feel genuinely earned.

items.source_lo: Student demonstrates critical listening comprehension by predicting and verifying answers to structured questions using a read-aloud story as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Ant's determination, roti too heavy to carry, bird building nest in wind, teamwork lifting roti, never-give-up message.
items.item_stem: In the story of the ant in the forest, what caused the ant to feel exhausted and saddened before she was inspired to try again?

options.label: A
options.text: Her fellow ants refused to help her carry the crumb.

options.label: B
options.text: She lost her way back to the anthill in the thick green forest.

options.label: C
options.text: She tried pushing, pulling, and rolling the piece of roti but could not move it alone.

options.label: D
options.text: The wind kept blowing the twigs and leaves away from her.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student has confused the forest setting detail with the ant's actual problem, showing imprecise listening.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has attributed the bird's difficulty to the ant, confusing the two creatures in the story.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has reversed the story's outcome — the ants do help — suggesting they missed or misheard the resolution.

items.source_lo: Student demonstrates critical listening comprehension by predicting and verifying answers to structured questions using a read-aloud story as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Ant's determination, roti too heavy to carry, bird building nest in wind, teamwork lifting roti, never-give-up message.
items.item_stem: In the ant's story, a small bird is trying to build a nest while the wind keeps blowing the twigs away. What did the bird's behaviour teach the ant, and how did that lesson change what the ant did next?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The bird's refusal to give up despite repeated setbacks showed the ant that persistence leads to success. Inspired by this, the ant stopped sitting in defeat and instead called her fellow ants for help; together they formed a chain and carried the roti back to the anthill.

items.item_stem: Using the seven-part structure you have practised — Introduction, Challenge, Feeling disheartened, Source of motivation, Action, Result, Reflection — recount a time when you faced a setback and chose to continue. Make sure your listener can clearly follow each stage of your experience.

expected_elements: Narration follows the seven-part sequence without skipping stages.
A specific, concrete challenge and motivation source are named.
Language is clear; sentences are mostly complete and connected.
A genuine reflection or insight closes the narration.

items.item_stem: King Bruce in the poem says, 'The spider up there defied despair; he conquered, and why shouldn't I?' Imagine you are speaking to a younger student who has just failed at something important. Using ideas from your own experience or from the poem, give your opinion — with at least one reason — on why giving up too soon is a mistake.

expected_elements: A clear opinion on why giving up too soon is a mistake is stated.
At least one reason is supported by a personal example or the poem.
The student addresses a younger audience in accessible, encouraging language.
The response shows awareness that failure can precede success.

items.item_stem: Write an informal letter to your cousin who is feeling discouraged after failing a school test. In your letter, give a step-by-step plan for overcoming the difficulty. Use the transition words 'To begin with', 'Next', 'After that', 'Then', and 'Finally' to sequence your advice. Use the correct informal letter format with address, date, salutation, body, and closing.

expected_elements: Correct informal letter format: address, date, salutation, body, closing.
All five transition words used to sequence a logical plan of steps.
Advice is specific and encouraging, not merely telling cousin to 'work hard'.
Friendly, warm register appropriate to writing to a cousin.

items.item_stem: In 'Try Again', the spider's nine failed attempts before it finally reached its cobweb home are what inspired King Bruce. Write a short imaginative paragraph (8–10 sentences) from the spider's point of view, describing what it thought and felt during those nine attempts. Your writing should show how the spider's determination grew rather than shrank with each fall.

expected_elements: First-person voice of the spider is sustained throughout.
Internal thoughts or feelings are expressed for at least two of the nine attempts.
Writing shows determination growing, not simply repeating the same feeling.
Imagery or specific details from the poem (thread, ceiling dome, cobweb) are woven in.

fast | fail

items.item_stem:
The poem describes the spider's climb using words that suggest hard, persistent effort. Choose the word from the brackets that best completes each sentence below, and write one original sentence of your own using the word 'endeavour' to show you understand its meaning.
(i) Every athlete must _____________ to improve every day, even after a poor performance. (toil / braced / strive)
(ii) Before stepping onto the stage, the young speaker _____________ herself with a deep breath and a quiet resolve. (endeavoured / braced / toiled)

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (i) strive — the word means to try very hard to achieve something, matching the athlete's ongoing effort. (ii) braced — the word means to prepare oneself for something difficult, fitting the speaker's act of steadying herself. Original sentence: any correct sentence using 'endeavour' in context, e.g. 'We must make every endeavour to finish our work before the deadline.'

items.item_stem: You have learned that spiders belong to a group called arachnids, not insects. Observe or recall what you know about a spider and an ant, and write four factual differences between them in the table below.
items.visual_stimulus:
Feature | Spider | Ant
Number of legs | | 
Number of body parts | | 
Group (insect/arachnid) | | 
Web-making ability | |

expected_elements: Spiders have eight legs; ants have six legs.
Spiders have two body parts; ants have three body parts.
Spiders are arachnids; ants are insects.
Spiders spin webs; ants do not spin webs.

items.source_context: Differences between spiders (arachnids) and ants; web-weaving craft decorated with words from 'Try Again'.
items.item_stem: Design a spider-web display that brings together science and the poem 'Try Again'. Your display should: (a) show the basic structure of a spider web with at least three labelled parts or features; (b) include at least four words or phrases from the poem that connect to the spider's journey (for example, 'strong endeavour', 'silken filmy clue'); and (c) include a two-sentence caption explaining what the spider in the poem and a real spider have in common. You may draw, write, or combine both.

expected_elements: Web diagram has at least three labelled structural features.
At least four poem phrases are placed on or around the web.
Caption connects real spider behaviour to the poem's perseverance theme.
Overall display shows a clear link between scientific observation and literary meaning.
